turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Morning. Obs are done. Blood pressure is 142 over 86, pulse 78, oxygen sat 96 percent. Weight today is 81 kilos.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right. In you come. What's the problem?
[SEG0003] person_3 (PATIENT): Umm. The cough.
[SEG0004] person_3 (PATIENT): Every morning there's this brown phlegm and it's been going forever and I'm worried sick about it.
[SEG0005] person_3 (PATIENT): Dad had the lung cancer. I keep thinking that's me. Is it cancer?
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): One thing at a time. The cough, every morning?
[SEG0007] person_3 (PATIENT): Yeah. Soon as I'm awake. Err I hack away for about ten minutes.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): And the phlegm's brown?
[SEG0009] person_3 (PATIENT): Brown. Like tea. Not blood. I check it every time.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any blood in it at all?
[SEG0011] person_3 (PATIENT): No. No blood.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Chest pain?
[SEG0013] person_3 (PATIENT): No chest pain. That's the one thing I haven't got.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Weight dropping?
[SEG0015] person_3 (PATIENT): No. Weight's steady.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): When did this cough start?
[SEG0017] person_3 (PATIENT): Umm I can't pin a date. Years. Maybe five, maybe longer. I don't know.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke?
[SEG0019] person_3 (PATIENT): I quit last year, in March. Before that thirty years, twenty cigarettes a day.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Still off them?
[SEG0021] person_3 (PATIENT): Yeah. Not one since.
[SEG0022] person_4 (CAREGIVER): True. No smokes in the house. I drive him in and I sort the tablets.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Which tablets?
[SEG0024] person_3 (PATIENT): Omprazole twenty milligrams every morning for the reflux. Mizartan 40 mg once a day for the pressure. And Metformine for the sugar, the diabetes.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): Dose of the Metformine?
[SEG0026] person_3 (PATIENT): 500 milligrams, twice a day. Morning and with tea.
[SEG0027] person_4 (CAREGIVER): He misses the evening Metformine though. Half the time it's still in the blister.
[SEG0028] person_3 (PATIENT): I do not. Well. Sometimes. Umm maybe I miss a few.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Stopped any?
[SEG0030] person_3 (PATIENT): The Seretide, purple puffer. I stopped it in March when I quit the smokes. They wanted atorvastatin as well but I never took that one.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): Bowels alright? Any change?
[SEG0032] person_3 (PATIENT): No. They're fine.
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): Fevers? Night sweats?
[SEG0034] person_3 (PATIENT): No. Neither of those.
[SEG0035] person_3 (PATIENT): Is brown phlegm always cancer? Do I need the scan today? What if it's already spread?
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not today. I'll listen to the chest.
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): Expiratory wheeze both sides. No crackles. Rest of the chest is clear.
[SEG0038] person_3 (PATIENT): Wheeze means COPD, doesn't it. Am I heading for oxygen? How worried should I be?
[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): I reckon chronic bronchitis from the smoking. Can't rule out COPD till we measure it.
[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): Spirometry next Tuesday arvo to check for the COPD. That's booked. Nurse takes bloods Thursday morning at eight, fasting. Full blood count and kidney function.
[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): If those are borderline we do the third test, the alpha-1. If the cough does not settle, a scan.
[SEG0042] person_3 (PATIENT): The alpha-1. What's that. Is that the cancer marker?
[SEG0043] person_2 (DOCTOR): No. It's a blood test for a rare cause of lung trouble. Only if the other two come back borderline.
[SEG0044] person_3 (PATIENT): Fast from midnight or what? Do I take the Mizartan? And the Omprazole? Will the Metformine wreck the numbers?
[SEG0045] person_2 (DOCTOR): Fast from midnight. Take the Mizartan and the Omprazole with a sip. Hold the Metformine till after the bloods.
[SEG0046] person_3 (PATIENT): And the vaccines. Should I get them? Which ones? Will they stir the cough up?
[SEG0047] person_2 (DOCTOR): Flu jab and the pneumonia one. Get both at the chemist.

[SEG0048] person_4 (CAREGIVER): I'll book the chemist on the way. Freeway was a shocker, mind you, forty minutes from Parramatta, and his grandson's cricket grand final is Saturday if the weather holds.
[SEG0049] person_3 (PATIENT): Little Jack bowls leg spin. Only nine. We were up early on the forecast. Meant to be sunny all weekend, he'll be filthy if it rains.
[SEG0050] person_2 (DOCTOR): Mm. I'll see you in two weeks with the results.
[SEG0051] person_3 (PATIENT): Two weeks. If I cough up blood before that, is it emergency or do I ring here? And can the wheeze just suddenly get worse?
[SEG0052] person_2 (DOCTOR): Blood, straight to emergency. Otherwise I'll see you in two weeks.
[SEG0053] person_1 (NURSE): Thursday morning, eight o'clock, fasting. I'll slot you in. Right.
[SEG0054] person_3 (PATIENT): Okay. Sorry about the hundred questions.
[SEG0055] person_2 (DOCTOR): Of.

symptoms.name: Morning cough
symptoms.frequency: every morning for about ten minutes

social_history.description: Quit in March last year after smoking 20 cigarettes a day for 30 years

clinical_assessment.basis: Cannot rule it out until spirometry

procedures_and_investigations.name: Fasting blood tests
procedures_and_investigations.normalized_name: Full blood count and kidney function

procedures_and_investigations.name: Scan
procedures_and_investigations.indication: if the cough does not settle

clinical_actions.description: Spirometry next Tuesday afternoon to check for COPD
Fasting bloods Thursday morning at eight for full blood count and kidney function; fast from midnight, take Mizartan and Omprazole with a sip, hold Metformine until after
Alpha-1 blood test if the other blood results are borderline
Scan if the cough does not settle
Get the influenza vaccine and the pneumococcal vaccine at the chemist
Go to emergency if coughing up blood
Follow-up consultation

clinical_uncertainties.description: The patient cannot say when the morning cough began.
The caregiver says the evening Metformine is missed about half the time and is often still in the blister, while the patient says he sometimes misses a few.

spec.situation: Former smoker who quit last year with a long-standing morning cough and brown phlegm; weight stable; no chest pain; spirometry planned; vaccination advice.

traps.happens: The transcript looks like speech-to-text: drug names are sometimes spelled wrongly ('Omprazole', 'Mizartan' for telmisartan, 'Metformine'), fragments and fillers appear ('Err', 'Of.', 'Mm.', 'Umm'), numbers are sometimes digits and sometimes words.
traps.label_rule: Medicine names are recorded as written in the transcript (name) with a normalized/generic name ONLY when the true drug is certain from context (a drug 'for the pressure' written 'Mizartan' is NOT certain enough: leave generic_name empty). Fragments and fillers are never facts.

traps.happens: In the plan the doctor books some tests or visits for a definite time ('the nurse takes bloods Thursday morning', 'I'll see you in two weeks') and makes others conditional ('if those are borderline we do the third test', 'if it does not settle, a scan').
traps.label_rule: Booked or arranged = status planned. Only the hedged ones are conditional. Never mark a booked test conditional or 'if needed'. Instructions for the booked test (fasting, time, medicine timing) belong to that test's action, not a separate invented plan item.

features: tangent_small_talk: a long tangent or small talk (traffic, cricket, the weather, a grandchild) that holds NO clinical content; nothing from it is extracted.

stopped_or_never_taken: a medicine the patient stopped, was never given or only took once ('I stopped it in March'). Status discontinued, not current; a medicine never taken is not recorded as a medication.

omissions.text: Morning cough produces brown/tea-coloured phlegm and the patient hacks for about 10 minutes soon after waking.
Caregiver reports the patient misses the evening metformin dose about half the time; evening tablet often still in the blister pack.
Atorvastatin was recommended previously but the patient never started/took it.
Doctor stated the rest of the chest examination was clear.
Planned blood tests are specifically full blood count and kidney function.
